content: Dental fear is the apprehension or anxiety associated with dental care and procedures. When this fear becomes pathological, it is classified as a specific phobia and is referred to by terms such as dental phobia, odontophobia, dentophobia, or dental anxiety. Studies suggest that up to 75% of adults in the United States experience some level of dental fear, ranging from mild unease to severe anxiety. Approximately 5-10% of adults in the U.S. suffer from dental phobia to the extent that they completely avoid dental care, even when it is necessary. These individuals often only seek dental treatment during emergencies, such as when they experience severe pain or develop a dental abscess. This avoidance behavior can create a cycle where fear leads to neglect of routine care, resulting in emergencies that require invasive procedures, which in turn reinforce the fear. Women are more likely to report dental fear than men, and younger individuals tend to be more affected than older adults. Fear is generally more pronounced for invasive procedures, such as oral surgery, compared to less invasive treatments like professional cleanings. The origins of dental fear are often linked to traumatic or painful past dental experiences. Additionally, hearing about others’ negative experiences or opinions about dentistry can contribute to the development of this fear. To address dental fear, a combination of behavioral and pharmacological approaches is commonly employed. Specialized clinics, such as those at the University of Washington in Seattle and Göteborg University in Sweden, integrate the expertise of psychologists and dentists to help patients manage and reduce their fear. These clinics aim to equip individuals with the skills necessary to undergo regular dental care with minimal anxiety. Outside of these specialized settings, many dental practitioners also use behavioral and cognitive strategies to help patients manage their fear. Behavioral treatments for dental fear often involve relaxation techniques, such as diaphragmatic breathing and progressive muscle relaxation, as well as cognitive strategies like cognitive restructuring and guided imagery. These methods have been shown to significantly alleviate dental anxiety. This technique involves gradually exposing the patient to the feared stimulus while teaching them relaxation skills to manage their anxiety. For instance, a patient with a fear of dental injections might first learn relaxation techniques and then be gradually introduced to the sight of a needle. Over time, the patient progresses to receiving an injection while using the relaxation skills, eventually achieving the ability to undergo the procedure with little to no fear. This method has proven effective in addressing specific fears, such as fear of injections. Pharmacological interventions are another option for managing dental fear and can range from mild sedation to general anesthesia. These methods are often used in conjunction with behavioral techniques. Nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas, is a frequently used sedative in dentistry. It is inhaled through a nasal mask and induces a state of relaxation and dissociation. Oral sedatives, such as benzodiazepines like alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), or triazolam (Halcion), may also be prescribed. These medications help patients feel calmer and sometimes drowsy during dental procedures, though they remain conscious and able to communicate. Intravenous (IV) sedation involves the administration of benzodiazepines directly into a vein, providing a deeper level of relaxation while the patient remains conscious and able to breathe independently. This is distinct from general anesthesia, where the patient is fully unconscious and requires assistance with breathing. For individuals who are fearful of dental care, finding a dentist who is experienced in working with anxious patients can be helpful. Recommendations from family, friends, dental insurance providers, or medical professionals can assist in identifying such practitioners. Some dentists advertise themselves as being gentle or catering to patients with dental anxiety. It is often recommended that individuals schedule an initial consultation with a new dentist to discuss their fears and past experiences without undergoing any treatment during that visit. Additionally, online support resources for dental fear have been found to be beneficial for some individuals.
